grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: Quiero leer. No puedo leer las letras pequeñas. Podemos escuchar a Rosa.
grammar.note_en:
Querer means “want”; poder means “can” or “be able to”. Before another verb, each takes an infinitive, the dictionary form ending in -ar, -er or -ir. The first verb changes to show who wants or can act; the infinitive stays unchanged. Quiero leer means “I want to read”; quiero entrar, “I want to enter”; puedo leer, “I can read”. Do not attach a personal ending to both verbs. The reading contrasts Rosa’s wish with the practical difficulty: Quiero leer mi libro, “I want to read my book”, but No puedo leer mi libro aquí, “I cannot read my book here”. Her difficulty with small print does not mean that she does not know how to read. She reads the large letters, chooses what she wants to hear and tells a story herself.

A stem is the part of a verb before its personal ending. The present forms shown here are irregular in their stems. Querer has quier- in quiero, quieres, quiere and quieren, but quer- in queremos. Poder has pued- in puedo, puedes, puede and pueden, but pod- in podemos. In queremos and podemos, the stem vowel is unstressed, and it keeps e or o rather than ie or ue. The endings still distinguish the speaker, listener or group: quiero/puedo, “I want/can”; quieres/puedes, familiar singular “you want/can”; quiere/puede, “he/she wants/can” and respectful singular “you want/can”; queremos/podemos, “we want/can”; quieren/pueden, “they want/can” and plural “you want/can”. Tenemos means “we have”, from tener; the earlier tienen means “they have” or plural “you have”. The new group form remains present tense. No other tense is introduced. The reference tables collect only these observed cells.

Podemos escuchar a Rosa means “We can listen to Rosa”. An infinitive can carry its own object: quiero contar la historia means “I want to tell the story”; podemos escuchar el cuento means “we can listen to the tale”. Contar here means “tell”, not “count”. The noun cuento means a tale; cuenta is also the third-person present of contar, “tells”. The financial noun cuenta from chapter 5 is a different word. Rosa cuenta la historia means “Rosa tells the story”; hay una cuenta vieja means “there is an old account”. Look at the sentence structure: a person telling something needs a verb, whereas una introduces a noun. The story also uses recuerdo, “I remember”, and recuerda, “she remembers”, from recordar. These selected present forms change o to ue. Saber appears as sé, “I know”, and sabe, “he/she knows”; sé has an accent. Yo sé el nombre de mi libro means “I know the name of my book”. This chapter does not ask for unseen forms of contar, recordar or saber.

Escuchar means “listen”. Luis lee en voz alta means “Luis reads aloud”; Rosa escucha a Luis means “Rosa listens to Luis”. Voz is voice, and alta in en voz alta describes audible reading rather than the physical height of an object. When a named person is the direct object—the person listened to or looked at—Spanish uses the personal a: escucha a Luis, “listens to Luis”; escucha a Rosa, “listens to Rosa”; mira a Elena, “looks at Elena”. It is not an extra English “to” in every construction, nor a new person doing the action. Ana escucha a Rosa has Ana as listener and Rosa as the person heard. The chapter confines this extension to named people; the existing location expressions remain separate.

Más means “more”: quiero leer más is “I want to read more”; hay más páginas, “there are more pages”; quiero escuchar más, “I want to listen to more”. This reading uses additional reading, listening and pages rather than a más … que comparison. Letras are printed characters or letters, not a written letter sent to someone. A página is a page. A cuento is a tale, here the fictional cat story in Rosa’s book; historia is the broader word “story”, used both for its sequence of events and Rosa’s new story. They overlap here without being interchangeable in every possible context. The earlier account, the reading-turn list and the name on another notebook page remain distinct pieces of writing.

Elena explicitly introduces Rosa, Ana and Luis before their conversation. The named neighbours then consistently use familiar singular tú forms, following the course’s after-introduction convention. Ana uses usted in her separate offer to the returning unnamed visitor, who remains unfamiliar to her: ¿Quiere usted otro papel? means “Would you like another paper?” This polite question uses the same present quiere as the third-person form. Ustedes remains the standard plural “you” in this Mexican dialogue. Subjects can be omitted when their verb endings and context identify them. The first speaker examples translate as follows: ¿Quieres leer el cartel? / ¿Puedes leer las letras?, “Do you want to read the sign? / Can you read the letters?”; Luis puede leer las letras pequeñas, “Luis can read the small letters”; nosotros queremos leer / podemos escuchar, “we want to read / we can listen”; ustedes quieren escuchar / pueden escuchar, “you want to listen / you can listen”. Rosa’s recognition of Elena’s name and a voice leaves the identity and history of that connection open; it does not establish a past-tense event or resolve the later photograph strand.

In the final form exercise, some cues give a personal form, such as escucha; others give an infinitive, such as escuchar. Use the sentence frame to choose the required form. After quiere or puede, return it to its infinitive: puede leer means “can read”, compared with lee, “reads”. Without a preceding modal, use the appropriate personal form: Ana escucha el cuento means “Ana listens to the tale”. Escuchar a Luis and escuchar a Ana mean “listen to Luis” and “listen to Ana”; the personal a marks the named person heard. The equivalent thing-object frame is escuchar el cuento, “listen to the tale”.
